items.title: Horn Shirley — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I‘m still with John Levy. We never had a contract. We shook hands; I guess I was eighteen. I was eighteen, yes.

ctx.x: How long were you with John Levy?

I‘m still with John Levy. We never had a contract. We shook hands; I guess I was eighteen. I was eighteen, yes. And I said, ―Are you going to be my manager?‖ Ai, yi, yi. But, you know, he had all the big people. He had the big acts. He tried. He tried. He tried hard. But when I said I‘m going to stay home and take care of my baby, you know, and I had to do that; I mean, it was no other way for me. I mean, I couldn‘t live with myself, because I‘d seen so many cases where, oh boy, it‘s sorry. And I‘m sorry, you…

Talk about . . . you touched on it, and then I want to go back to the Verve recordings, but you just talked about the decision to stay home. Was there one incident that prompted that, or was it just a feeling that it was really time, and Rainy was at a critical point?

items.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: “Here’s to Life” we had that tune for years before Shirley Horn recorded it

ctx.x: Yeah. All you could hear was his voice, and you know, he’d sing like “A Pretty Girl Is Like a Melody,” and these girls would walk around. And you never saw him. And he’d go on the air, like I think he was with Jimmy Noone. And he’d go on the air and sing nothing but ballads you know, just nothing but pretty tunes. But nobody paid any attention to that. A recording company didn’t want to know about that. They didn’t want to record Joe doing any ballads or anything. Right up until the last few years, we had to…

Because when he started out, actually RCA Victor did do some really beautiful things with big bands and strings and things. They never did anything with the records, but you know, this was the era of “A Man Ain’t Supposed To Cry” I think, and some of those things that they did in those days. But they never did anything with them. Because they were pretty ballad things, and they didn’t know how to promote them, they just satisfied Joe, you know.

items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He was the producer on them, although he didn’t show up. I ended up being the producer.

ctx.x: You mentioned Quincy Jones. When did you meet Quincy? How did you meet him? How did – I’m assuming that you knew him . . .

I just knew Quincy as a musician first. That’s my first thing to him. Then later, when he became an executive in the record business, I first met him, because Cannonball worked things with him or did things for him. I got to know him altogether from that time. But I knew him as a musician, as a player, when he [was in] Lionel Hampton’s band, and I knew him when he went out on the road and got stranded in Europe with the band. Some of the musicians that played were in the band. This is how I got to know him. Then…
You were also neighbors? Were you neighbors?
